item.title: Is AI Disclosure Day here?
item.dc:creator: Whizy Kim
item.description: Anthropic is adding watermarks to AI text generated by Claude—and other AI labs could soon follow suit.
item.content:encoded:
TL;DR: Anthropic will embed a new AI watermark in all text generated by Claude—and it may not be that easy to remove. It’s doing this to comply with an EU law that just went into effect, but it also lands as public fatigue around AI-made content reaches an all-time high.

What happened: This is good news for haters of AI writing, as the imperceptible watermark won’t get stripped out by copying and pasting.

Anthropic dropped the news yesterday, and it’s a glimpse of the impact the EU’s new AI transparency law might have. The law, which went into effect on August 2, requires providers of AI tools to mark their outputs in a “machine-readable format.” Anthropic is rolling out the watermark worldwide for all new models, and will eventually add it to existing ones.

The announcement comes as backlash against AI slop reaches critical mass, with platforms rolling out new features to label AI content seemingly every day. We don’t know exactly what Anthropic’s watermark will look like, but the system could be similar to Google’s SynthID, which works on text, images, videos, and audio. Another unanswered question: how detection tools will be made available to the public. Anthropic says it’s working on letting users and “other third parties” detect its watermark, as part of a voluntary Code of Practice the company recently signed.

How it (probably) works: AI text watermarks get embedded in the actual sequence of words—they’re not some invisible character you can remove by, say, manually retyping the text.

At a basic level, AI text generation works by predicting which word is statistically most likely to follow the previous one. But don’t worry, em-dash stans—your writing probably won’t get flagged just for sounding vaguely AI. These watermarks deploy a secret key that tweaks the probability of words used (leaving a signature that it was generated by a certain lab’s models)—and text that doesn’t match that pattern won’t carry the mark.

The big but: AI text watermarks aren’t tamper-proof. One study from Queen’s University found that paraphrasing with another AI model or using back translation—translating text into another language, then back to the original—could reduce detection of watermarked text. Or you could just dilute the AI text by dropping it into a larger body of human-written words so it’s harder to find.

Bottom line: Most major AI labs signed the same Code of Practice that Anthropic did—notable absences include Amazon and xAI—and everyone has to follow the new EU transparency rules. It could all usher in a drastic change for how AI text gets disclosed. And perhaps even how many AI slop books we see on digital shelves. —WK

item.title: Data center states are banning data centers
item.dc:creator: Lindsey Choo
item.description: Data center bans and protests are mounting even as Amazon bankrolls the US’s largest gas plant for its new AI campus.
item.content:encoded:
TL;DR: The data center ban count just topped 500 across the US—mostly in states where data centers already are. The bans come as protests mount and Amazon backs a Texas gas plant permitted to emit a record amount of pollution.

What happened: More than 500 US towns and counties have now blocked or restricted new data center developments, with New York and Texas the latest to pump the brakes statewide. The bans have been growing exponentially—the number jumped from 300 in late June to over 500 in July.

More than 400 of the restrictions sit in the Midwest and South, the two leading regions for data center buildouts. Texas Gov. Greg Abbott announced a moratorium on all data center approvals last week—until state regulators audit every project seeking a connection to its power grid. Nearly three-quarters of July’s moratoriums landed in southern states like Georgia and Florida. Perhaps not surprising, given Georgia ranks fourth with 276 existing and planned data centers. (Texas ranks second after Virginia with 537.)

Clapbacks: Meanwhile, data center critics are increasingly taking their objections to the streets. Last month, organizers held 142 protests across 42 states (Texas led with 18 protests). At least 37 arrests have been made at data center-related protests this year, per Futurism—and there were another 12 cases of police stepping in to keep protesters away from officials. (In one instance, a person was arrested for merely clapping at a meeting.)

Pollution mogging: The pushback comes amid growing concerns over data centers’ climate and power effects. On Friday, Amazon confirmed it’s investing in a new Texas AI campus whose gas plant is permitted to emit up to 33 million tons of carbon dioxide each year—roughly double the emissions of the country’s dirtiest coal plant. That’s equivalent to driving 7 million cars every year, or nearly 5% of Canada’s total emissions. The project “would not initially connect to the wider electricity grid,” an Amazon spokeswoman said, escaping the purview of the Texas moratorium.

Bottom line: Data centers are getting hit from every direction, from local bans to statewide freezes to protests. Whether any of it slows the rapid buildout is the big question. —LC

Also in data centers…

  • AI’s appetite for chips is driving a new lobbying blitz in DC.

item.title: AI just created viruses from scratch
item.dc:creator: Lindsey Choo
item.description: Researchers used AI to design new viruses. They also had to design their own safety guardrails.
item.content:encoded:
TL;DR: For the first time ever, scientists say they’ve taught AI to create brand-new viruses. The breakthrough could offer a new route for treating infections that antibiotics can’t touch, but you can probably guess the downsides…

What happened: In a new study published in Science yesterday, researchers at Stanford University and the Arc Institute showed that they used AI to write new viral genomes—first by teaching it to recognize the DNA structure of natural viruses, then asking it for blueprints that don’t exist. The team’s AI models, Evo 1 and Evo 2, trained on a massive library of genetic data, then specifically on viruses related to Phi X-174, a natural virus that only infects the E. coli bacteria.

Of the 700,000 potential viruses generated by Evo, nearly 300 were built in the lab, and 16 turned out to be viable. (Some multiplied even faster than Phi X-174.)

Why it matters: A mixture of the AI-designed viruses overcame E. coli strains that had learned to fend off Phi X-174 (which a comparable mix of natural viruses couldn’t do). It’s an early proof of concept that AI could be used to treat drug-resistant bacterial infections. It’s also a turning point for AI use in biology, as models move from analyzing and predicting genomes to writing complete, functional ones.

Voluntary safety: As anyone who saw the Bond movie No Time to Die knows, engineered bioweapon plots don’t end well. And right now, the only thing keeping that scenario fictional is the honor system. The researchers in the study wanted to be “extra careful” about the potential of generating genomes of viruses that could harm humans, and deliberately excluded viruses that could infect humans, animals, and plants from the training data.

Health security scientists at Johns Hopkins, who weren’t involved in the study, commended the team on the precautionary step. As they put it, “The ability to compose viral genomes using generative AI now exists; the governance to safely steer it does not.”

Bottom line: The models are a step toward new treatments, but they’re also a preview of the next AI safety fight. For now, the only guardrail is what a research team decides not to teach its model. —LC

item.title: Google’s AI godfathers are logging off
item.dc:creator: Whizy Kim
item.description: Jeff Dean and Demis Hassabis stepped back from their roles at Google on the same day, capping a few months of AI talent bleed at the company.
item.content:encoded:
TL;DR: Some of Google’s brightest minds in AI have headed for the exits in the last few months—including two big shakeups yesterday. This could all be a symptom of a company that now appears less interested in bleeding-edge AI research, and more in selling Gemini seats.

What happened: Google dropped two bombshells yesterday. The first: Jeff Dean—the firm’s chief scientist and a 27-year company veteran—is leaving to start his own company. And Demis Hassabis, who co-founded the cutting-edge AI lab DeepMind in 2010, is stepping down as CEO to become the division’s chair and Alphabet’s chief scientist, which will mean less day-to-day management.

This latest shakeup caps a brutal few months of departures for Google, including Gemini’s co-lead Noam Shazeer announcing in June that he’s off to OpenAI. Shazeer is co-author of the paper that invented the transformer behind modern LLMs—the “T” in ChatGPT.

Some behind-the-scenes tea: The one-two punch yesterday shocked the wider tech industry, but apparently not people inside Google, per tech reporter Alex Heath. Hassabis started taking a step back at least a year ago, according to Semafor, and “struggled to get satisfaction out of being in the role of a tech executive, rather than a visionary scientist.”

There are also multiple reports of falling morale: CNBC notes that Google’s researchers are frustrated by the company selling precious compute to other AI labs like Anthropic, limiting the pursuit of their own projects. Insiders told Axios that the vibes are bad enough that they’re delaying model releases.

From moonshots to Gemini licenses: Lately, Google has focused on growing its Cloud business, which includes Gemini Enterprise—something CEO Sundar Pichai boasts that 90% of Fortune 100 companies now use. Google might also spend as much as $205 billion on capex this year, much of it likely on data centers to further expand its cloud compute arm.

Some read all this as a sign that Google is letting its AGI-chasing research fall to the wayside, content to ship “good enough” models that fulfill the needs of most consumers and firms. (In a blog post about Hassabis’s role change, Pichai said Google is “committed to being at the frontier” while also touting its “incredible momentum at earnings.”)

Bottom line: This might be Google’s Ship of Theseus moment. Plank by plank, a company whose researchers once put it at the forefront of the gen AI race is rebuilding itself around selling compute to its frontier rivals. —WK

Also at Google…

  • Agentic AI comes to Google Maps, now letting you order food and book hotels straight from the app.

item.title: The White House sets open weights free
item.dc:creator: Whizy Kim
item.description: The US government finalized its AI review framework this week—and it apparently leaves out open-weight models. We have a lot of questions.
item.content:encoded:
TL;DR: After two months, the White House’s voluntary AI review framework has been finalized—but we don’t get to know exactly what’s in it. One detail that has leaked: It doesn’t cover open-weight models. This may be a sign that, after the recent hullabaloo around Chinese versions, the Trump administration wants more homegrown open models.

What happened: The age of (voluntary) AI oversight is here—and so far it’s mainly been…confusing. The latest example: The White House doesn’t plan to publicly release its AI review framework, per Axios—though it held closed-door meetings with AI companies to discuss it yesterday. It’s a move that one critic called “baffling,” and some elected officials have called for more clarity around the government’s whiplash-inducing approach to regulating AI overall (including its abrupt export control order on Fable and Mythos in June).

This new framework would evaluate the cyber capabilities of AI models before they’re publicly released. Among the few morsels that insiders revealed: It only covers closed-source “state-of-the-art” models that pose a national security risk. But what “state of the art” means—and why open-weight models aren’t included—is a little murky.

A win for the open-weight camp?: The White House hasn’t commented on the open-weight exclusion, but there are probably a few reasons for the move. For one, anyone can download open weights and remove any safeguards, making a government safety review pretty toothless (especially one that’s voluntary).

But likely the bigger reason? Leaving out open weights might encourage US companies to build more of them, competing against China’s flood of cheaper, increasingly capable open models. In a recent interview, National Cyber Director Sean Cairncross said the administration is “extremely interested in looking at ways to build US open source” and make it “the preferential adoption by planet Earth.” All this means Jensen Huang is probably having a great day—Dario Amodei, maybe not so much.

Bottom line: There hasn’t been much clarity around the White House’s regulation of AI—including whether its review scheme is truly “voluntary”—but the government is apparently trying to walk a fine line between oversight and innovation. At least for now. —WK

item.title: Google exec says link lists aren’t going away as search transforms
item.dc:creator: Patrick Kulp
item.description: Google VP of Search Liz Reid discussed how the search experience is changing in the AI era and what it means for the internet as a whole.
item.content:encoded:
In recent months, AI has fundamentally changed what it means to google something—and the transformation isn’t done.

The search engine made a slew of announcements at its developer conference earlier this year that included the first change to the search box in a quarter century. The upshot is a more AI-centric experience with options for news alert-style information agents that automatically scour the web for you.

Though Google has clarified that the familiar list of links isn’t going away, multiple headlines have called it the end of search as we know it. But Reid insisted that Google still cares about the health of the internet as a whole.

“Search is not a useful product if the web is not a thriving product, and so I think we probably care about that more than any other company in the world,” Google VP of Search Liz Reid told us.

We spoke with Reid about what this means for how you browse the web, what it means for websites that depend on Google for survival, and how it will change the ads you see.

This interview has been edited for length and clarity.

Do you think that there’s a time in the future, amid all this AI change, that the familiar list of links could go away entirely? Or that there could be a different format for funneling users to the web?

I don’t see any time in which the links go away. I think what we actually see is that people don’t want AI or the web; they want both. There’s a lot of topics where AI really gets you started, and then people want to engage more. They value the expertise, the opinions, the taste of how to think about a particular topic. This is a time in which AI is growing, and it’s a time in which newsletters and podcasts and videos and all these new formats seem to also be blossoming because people really want to hear that expertise. So we want to continue to make that thrive.

We have for a long time continued to innovate on how you can surface links on the web. So we have the blue links, but we have, at times, we have the top stories part. We have what people are saying in AI Mode and in AI Overviews.

If we know users want to connect to that information, how do we make it as easy as possible? How do we make it as seamless as possible? And we’ll continue to innovate and we announced some updates pretty recently on how we’re showcasing links in additional ways. But I think that is kind of what makes search at its heart—not just knowing the information about the web, but connecting people to content on the web. And I don’t see that going away.

Obviously, online publishers are seeing click-through rates decline with these changes, and some publishers are even considering blocking all Google crawlers. In terms of making sure that the open web is still a healthy place to supply these AI tools and search, how do you think about that in the long term?

We do spend a lot of time thinking about this. We try to really design our AI experiences in sort of a web-forward way. We have teams whose job is to think about: What are great links to surface more effectively? How do you show them in a way that’s great for folks? We’ve innovated; one example is in AI Overviews, we’ll now often show on some timely stories, a big carousel of publishers that we didn’t have three months ago. So we’re constantly trying to figure out how we innovate on that.

The good news is that people still want to connect with other people’s content, and so we can facilitate that. And as long as people make great content that other people want to read, then we believe we can continue to foster that.

Companies like Microsoft are experimenting with publisher marketplaces or other compensation schemes. Is that something you’re considering?

We have a blog post in which we’ve talked about some of the various news deals and other things we have.

We have a variety of different ways—we have a long history of deals with news and others for great content. In general, we’re all still—I mean, at times it can feel like a long time—but we’re still pretty early in the space, and so continue to innovate.

In terms of the revenue side, how has this changed Google’s ad model? Do you feel like you’ve kind of cracked advertising in generative AI?

What we are seeing is as people ask longer queries, they’re specifying more of their intent. What are they really trying to do? What’s important to them? And that sort of allows new opportunities to think about ads targeting.

There’s some efforts like direct offers, in which…the advertiser can give a more specific ad for you based on what it is. And so, an example is like you’re searching for a hotel, you’re searching with a family. Maybe a hotel wants to offer free breakfast. They’re not going to give free breakfast to the person that they think is traveling for business who will just pay, or they won’t eat. But this family might pick that hotel because of it, and so Google’s system will allow [the hotel] to say, “Oh, I have a special discount just for you for breakfast,” and that really provides new value to the user and sort of allows the hotel to get additional visitors. We both have something that’s working, and there’s lots of room for innovation going forward.

There’s always been some level of slop on the internet, and I know Google has tools to sift through that. But as generative AI tools have created this ability to churn out more content, how do you make sure that with things like the AI Overviews, the accuracy is maintained? And have you seen the accuracy of those go up overall?

To your point, there’s always been slop. Sometimes people are like, “Oh, there’s now slop on the web.” In my experience, there’s been slop for 20 years. So we have a lot of experience and teams whose job is to ensure that both we’re getting rid of spam and that that rarely surfaces, and that high-quality content continues to surface. And when we do AI Overviews or AI Mode, we actually make use of those underlying search ranking systems so that it’s the highest-quality sites going into AI Overviews. Overall, the quality of the AI Overviews has continued to improve and has improved considerably since we first launched. The models are much better, for one, so that really helps. But also, we’ve just learned a lot and continue to grow on what the techniques are [and] how you work with the models to ensure that you can actually really ground the data in high-quality information.

Are Gemini and AI Mode search still different experiences, or are they converging into the same thing?

We think of them as having two different North Stars. Gemini is really focused on being this assistant, and search AI Mode is really focused on a generative AI search experience. And so for search, that means the importance of connecting to the web is vital. And so the way that we show the web is different…we tend to focus on information use cases more heavily. Versus with Gemini, we’ll focus on a lot of productivity and creativity use cases.

The use cases overlap. We have a view that you should meet users where you are, so you don’t go and say, like, “Oops, you asked the question in the wrong product. Try again.” We will try and answer across both of them the full breadth of questions that come to our products, but we will tune them differently, and really tune search to focus on optimizing for information use cases and optimizing for connecting people to the web.

Where is Google search headed in the long term, and what are some of the biggest ways we can expect it to change further?

There’s a couple of things that we see. Experiences are becoming more personal and custom for you, for each one. It’s not just that you can ask that longer question, but that we start to understand how to make information most useful for you. We see people learn differently. We have people who love videos and people who hate videos. We have people who are experts in the financial jargon and not in the medical jargon. We have people who speak different languages.

And so, with some of the things like generative UI…the job is not just for you to technically access information, but for it to be useful to you—that’s an important part of the mission. How do we present information in ways that are much more useful? That sense of building a thing that feels designed for you, and not just designed for 2 billion people, to make it easier for you to understand and grasp the information will continue.

Also, agents and how they show up in search in terms of just, how do they offload more of the work you don’t want to do? I think people have parts of searching where they enjoy and they’re delighted, and then they have parts of tasks that feel like there’s a lot of toil. And so, how can you offload those parts, and then make it easy for people to spend their time on the things they want to enjoy?

We’ll see that people will ask harder and harder questions. That’s been the evolution of search. You get better at answering the question. They’re like, “OK, I’m gonna raise the bar on you,” and so I think we’ll continue to see people go more and more to, what’s the real question they’re trying to get done, what’s the task they’re trying to get done.

item.title: This startup wants a robot to change your tires
item.dc:creator: Jordyn Grzelewski
item.description: One of the problems ATI aims to help solve is a growing shortage of automotive service technicians.
item.content:encoded:
Getting your car’s tires changed is the automotive service equivalent of getting a root canal.

That’s how Andy Chalofsky, CEO of newly launched AI and robotics company Automated Tire, Inc., or ATI, thinks of it—and why he and his fellow co-founders decided to use an emerging technology to disrupt a process that’s historically been cumbersome, time-consuming, and physically demanding.

“While the auto industry has made great strides with advanced technologies over recent decades, automotive service bays have seen little innovation to match,” Chalofsky said in a statement Tuesday announcing ATI’s emergence from stealth.

“Most notably, electric vehicles wear through tires up to 30% faster,” he added. “The proliferation of EVs creates significantly more tire service opportunities, but tire technician jobs are dirty, injury-prone, and difficult to fill.”

Get smart: Enter SmartBay, ATI’s platform that uses robotics, machine learning, and computer vision to automate services including tire changes, wheel balancing, and vehicle inspections. The startup touts SmartBay as a way to increase repair shops’ efficiency, improve the customer experience, and help solve a nagging automotive technician shortage.

Here’s how it works: Once a vehicle is in position, the platform automatically begins an inspection. It analyzes tire and wheel conditions while gathering diagnostic data. “The robotic system then executes the tire change and wheel balancing process, removing and reinstalling tires with consistent accuracy while simultaneously calculating and applying precise wheel weights to ensure optimal balance,” according to a news release.

According to ATI, SmartBay allows one technician to manage up to three service bays at a time, reducing the time for a full tire service job by half. The product fits within a standard 12-foot service bay.

So tire-d: Chalofsky represents the fourth generation of his family to work in the tire business. He started working in tire distribution and went on to establish an online tire retailer that he later sold. In 2020, he said, he started to think about the next industry challenge he wanted to focus on.

“We just saw that there was a real need in installation, and tire changing and wheel balancing,” he told us. “It’s not a very pleasurable customer experience. We would talk to the shops and the shops would oftentimes talk about how hard it was to get labor.”

ATI cited a report from the National Automotive Dealers Association identifying a shortage of 37,000 automotive service technicians. This shortage affects drivers, ATI argued, by leading to “inconsistent service quality and even more grueling wait times.”

“We’re making not only that technician more efficient—we’re making them more profitable for them and the shop. And we’re also making it an easier job with a lower threshold of skill,” Chalofsky said. “You’re now taking the workforce and you’re allowing them to fill in the gap a little bit and do a job they’d actually rather do.”

He noted that repair shops and dealers employ highly skilled mechanics who are trained to work on vehicles that are becoming ever more complex. Rather than having these skilled workers do tire changes and vehicle inspections, they can focus on more lucrative and specialized service jobs.

“By segmenting that work, we’re allowing those…technicians to really focus on the more complicated vehicles and the more complicated problems,” Chalofsky said.

Problem, meet solution: Chalofsky believes that starting with a problem, then devising a solution, differentiates ATI’s approach from other tech startups.

“The most common tech story is these smart people that are into robotics or into engineering. They’re solving problems, and then they’re taking it to an industry to try to get a product-market fit,” he said. “The thing that defines us is the opposite: We have robotics and engineering talent, of course, but are really founded with deep automotive tire expertise. And we focused on solving a problem and bringing engineering to that problem, rather than engineering and then trying to bring the industry to the problem.”

item.title: SMB tech buyers: Ready for the next wave?
item.dc:creator: Morning Brew Creative Studio
item.description: See if your current tech matches up to modern PCs
item.content:encoded:
From budget cycles to contract renewals to pain points that force a switch, a company tech buyers’ schedule isn’t set in stone. But if you’re a small-to-medium-sized (SMB) tech buyer currently wondering what your next buying cycle should include, we teamed up with Snapdragon to help you better understand your org’s potential tech needs, gaps, and compatibility. After these seven questions, you’ll know if your tech is equipped, if it’s time to take inventory, or if you should consider a PC refresh, pronto. Let’s get into it.


*Performance is based on Cinebench Single Core run in Windows 11. Snapdragon X Elite (X1E-80-100) was tested using a Dell XPS 13 (9345). The Intel Core Ultra 7 256V was tested using a Dell XPS 13 (9350). On battery performance measured on “Balanced” Power Mode in Windows and “Optimized” in Dell Power Manager for both devices. Power and performance comparison reflects results based on measurements and hardware instrumentation of given devices; results may vary based on device power settings and/or OEM configurations. Battery life varies significantly with device, settings, usage, and other factors.

Snapdragon is a product of Qualcomm Technologies, Inc. and/or its subsidiaries.
